source_refs.note: Chapter 2 exercise (PDF 51-53, printed 48-50), solved: each MCQ carries its key worked out from the chapter (the book prints no key), and the short, constructed response and comprehensive questions and numerical problems carry model answers. Two printed numerical answers are corrected (2.6, 2.8).

blocks.prompt: 2.1 The angle at which dot product becomes equal to cross product:
blocks.explanation: AB cos θ = AB sin θ gives tan θ = 1, so θ = 45°.

blocks.prompt: 2.2 The projectile gains its maximum height at an angle of:
blocks.explanation: Height h = vi² sin²θ / 2g is greatest when sin θ = 1, i.e. θ = 90° (thrown vertically up).

blocks.prompt: 2.3 The scalar product of two vector is maximum if they are:
blocks.explanation: A.B = AB cos θ is greatest when cos θ = 1 (θ = 0°), i.e. for parallel vectors: A.B = AB.

blocks.prompt: 2.4 The range of projectile is same for two angles which are mutually:
blocks.explanation: R = vi² sin 2θ / g, and sin 2(90° - θ) = sin (180° - 2θ) = sin 2θ. So complementary angles (θ and 90° - θ, e.g. 30° and 60°) give the same range.

blocks.prompt: 2.5 The acceleration at the top of a trajectory of projectile is:
blocks.explanation: At the top the vertical velocity is zero, but gravity still acts, so the acceleration is g (9.8 m s⁻², downward) at every point of the path.

blocks.prompt: 2.6 SI unit of impulse is:
blocks.explanation: Impulse = F × t, so its unit is newton second (N s), the same as kg m s⁻¹ (the unit of momentum).

blocks.prompt: 2.7 The rate of change of momentum is:
blocks.explanation: Newton's second law in terms of momentum: the time rate of change of momentum of a body is equal to the applied force, F = (mvf - mvi)/t.

blocks.prompt: 2.8 As rocket moves upward during its journey, then its acceleration goes on:
blocks.explanation: a = mv/M. As the fuel burns and is ejected, the mass M of the rocket decreases, so its acceleration increases (2.12).

blocks.prompt: 2.9 Elastic collision involves:

options.text: no gain, no loss of energy
no relation between energy and elastic collision

blocks.explanation: In a perfectly elastic collision no kinetic energy is lost: the total K.E. (and momentum) before and after the collision is the same.

blocks.prompt: 2.1 State right hand rule for two vectors w.r.t. vector product.
blocks.explanation:
Place the tails of A and B together. Rotate the first vector A into B through the smaller angle and curl the fingers of the right hand in the direction of rotation, keeping the thumb erect.
The erect thumb gives the direction of A × B, perpendicular to the plane of A and B.

blocks.prompt: 2.2 Define impulse and show how it is related to momentum.
blocks.explanation:
Impulse is the product of the average force F and the time t for which it acts: Impulse = F × t (unit N s).
From Newton's second law F = (mvf - mvi)/t, so F × t = mvf - mvi.
Impulse = change in momentum.

blocks.prompt: 2.3 Differentiate between an elastic and an inelastic collision.
blocks.explanation: In both, momentum and total energy are conserved; the difference is whether kinetic energy is conserved.

rows: Kinetic energy of the system is conserved
Kinetic energy of the system is not conserved
No K.E. is lost in the collision
Part of the K.E. changes into heat, sound and deformation
Example: hard ball dropped on a marble floor rebounds almost to its height
Example: bullet fired into a block of wood; colliding tennis balls

blocks.prompt: 2.4 Show that rate of change in momentum is equal to force applied. Also state Newton's second law of motion in terms of momentum.
blocks.explanation:
A force F acts on mass m for time t and changes its velocity from vi to vf: a = (vf - vi)/t and, by Newton's second law, a = F/m.
So F/m = (vf - vi)/t, or F = (mvf - mvi)/t: force = rate of change of momentum.
Newton's second law: the time rate of change of momentum of a body is equal to the applied force.

blocks.prompt: 2.5 State law of conservation of linear momentum. Also state condition under which it holds.
blocks.explanation:
Law: the total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant, i.e. m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v₁′ + m₂v₂′.
Condition: the system must be isolated: no external force acts on it (only internal action-reaction forces, which cancel).

blocks.prompt: 2.6 Show that range of projectile is maximum at an angle of 45°.
blocks.explanation:
Range R = (vi²/g) sin 2θ. For a given vi, R is maximum when sin 2θ = 1 (its largest value).
So 2θ = 90°, or θ = 45°, and Rmax = vi²/g.

blocks.prompt: 2.7 Find the time of flight of a projectile to reach the maximum height.
blocks.explanation:
At the maximum height the vertical velocity becomes zero: vfy = vi sin θ - gt = 0.
So t = vi sin θ / g, which is half of the total time of flight T = 2vi sin θ / g.

blocks.prompt: 2.8 The maximum horizontal range of a projectile is 800 m. Find the value of height attained by the projectile at θ = 60°.
blocks.explanation:
Rmax = vi²/g = 800 m, so vi² = 800 m × g.
h = vi² sin²θ / 2g = (800 m × g)(sin 60°)² / 2g = 800 m × 0.75 / 2
h = 300 m

blocks.prompt: 2.1 Why does a hunter aiming a bird in a tree miss the target exactly at the bird?
blocks.explanation:
The bullet becomes a projectile as soon as it leaves the gun. It moves forward with constant horizontal velocity, but gravity pulls it down at the same time (vertical fall y = ½gt²).
So it falls below the straight line of aim and passes under the bird, which stays where it was. To hit, the hunter must aim slightly above the bird.

blocks.prompt: 2.2 A person falling on a heap of sand does not hurt more as compared to a person falling on a concrete floor. Why?
blocks.explanation:
In both cases the person's momentum changes by the same amount (from mv to zero), and F × t = change in momentum.
Sand gives way, so the person stops in a longer time t and the force F = Δp/t on the body is small.
Concrete stops the person almost at once (very small t), so the force is very large and hurts more.

blocks.prompt: 2.3 State the conditions under which birds fly in air.
blocks.explanation:
A bird flaps its wings and pushes air downward and backward; by Newton's third law (conservation of momentum) the air pushes the bird upward and forward.
Conditions:
1. Air must be present for the wings to push against (a bird cannot fly in a vacuum).
2. The upward push of the air (lift) must be equal to or greater than the bird's weight.
3. The forward push (thrust) must overcome the air resistance (drag).
(beyond the chapter: the chapter does not discuss flight.)

blocks.prompt:
2.4 Describe the circumstances for which velocity and acceleration of a vehicle are:
(i) v is zero but a is not zero
(ii) a is zero but v is not zero
(iii) perpendicular to one another
blocks.explanation:
(i) v = 0, a ≠ 0: a vehicle at the instant it starts from rest (or the instant it reverses direction); likewise a body thrown up has v = 0 at the top while a = g.
(ii) a = 0, v ≠ 0: a vehicle moving with uniform velocity (constant speed in a straight line).
(iii) v ⊥ a: a vehicle going round a circular track at constant speed: the velocity is along the tangent and the acceleration is towards the centre.

blocks.prompt: 2.5 Describe briefly effects of air resistance on the range of a projectile.
blocks.explanation:
Air resistance slows down the forward motion of the projectile and reduces its velocity, so its range (and height) decreases.
Air resistance is not constant: as the projectile slows down it also decreases. So the path is not a perfect parabola but is skewed, with a steeper descent than ascent, and falls short of the ideal parabolic path.

blocks.prompt: 2.1 Define and explain scalar product. Write down its important characteristics.
blocks.explanation:
Definition: if the product of two vectors is a scalar quantity, it is called the scalar (dot) product:
A.B = AB cos θ
where A and B are the magnitudes of the vectors and θ is the angle between them.
Explanation: bring A and B to a common origin. Then
A.B = A (projection of B on A) = A (B cos θ) = AB cos θ
Similarly B.A = B (A cos θ) = BA cos θ.
Example: work done by a force F moving its point of application through d at angle θ: W = (F cos θ) d = F.d.
Characteristics:
1. Commutative: A.B = B.A (the order does not matter).
2. Perpendicular vectors (θ = 90°): A.B = AB cos 90° = 0.
3. Parallel vectors (θ = 0°): A.B = AB (maximum); antiparallel (θ = 180°): A.B = -AB.
4. Self product: A.A = A².
5. In rectangular components: A.B = AxBx + AyBy + AzBz.
6. The angle between two vectors: cos θ = (AxBx + AyBy + AzBz)/AB.

blocks.prompt: 2.2 Define and explain vector product of two vectors. Discuss important characteristic of vector product.
blocks.explanation:
Definition: if the product of two vectors is a vector quantity, it is called the vector (cross) product:
A × B = AB sin θ n̂
where θ is the angle between A and B, and n̂ is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane containing A and B.
Direction (right hand rule): place the tails of A and B together, rotate A into B through the smaller angle and curl the fingers of the right hand in that direction; the erect thumb gives the direction of A × B. Hence B × A is opposite to A × B.
Characteristics:
1. Non-commutative: A × B ≠ B × A; in fact A × B = -B × A.
2. Perpendicular vectors (θ = 90°): magnitude is maximum, A × B = AB n̂.
3. Parallel or antiparallel vectors (θ = 0° or 180°): A × B = 0 (null vector); so A × A = 0.
4. The magnitude of A × B equals the area of the parallelogram with A and B as adjacent sides.
Examples:
Torque: τ = r × F
Force on a charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B: F = q(v × B)

blocks.prompt: 2.3 Derive three equations of motion by graphical method.
blocks.explanation:
Velocity-time graph: a body moves with constant acceleration a; its velocity changes from vi (point A, OA = vi) to vf (point B) in time t. Draw BD perpendicular to the time axis (BD = vf, OD = t) and AC parallel to the time axis, meeting BD at C (AC = OD = t, CD = OA = vi). AB is a straight line.
First equation (vf = vi + at):
BD = BC + CD = BC + OA, so vf = BC + vi ...... (1)
Slope of AB = acceleration: a = BC/AC = BC/t, so BC = at ...... (2)
From (1) and (2): vf = vi + at
Second equation (S = vit + ½at²):
Distance S = area under the graph OABD = area of rectangle OACD + area of triangle ABC
S = (OA × OD) + ½(AC × BC) = vi t + ½(t × at)
S = vit + ½at²
Third equation (2aS = vf² - vi²):
S = area of trapezium OABD = ½(sum of parallel sides) × height = ½(OA + BD) × OD
S = ½(vi + vf) t
From the first equation t = (vf - vi)/a, so
S = ½(vf + vi)(vf - vi)/a
2aS = vf² - vi²
These equations apply only to motion in a straight line with constant acceleration.

blocks.prompt: 2.4 What is projectile motion? Explain.
blocks.explanation:
Definition: projectile motion is two-dimensional motion under constant acceleration due to gravity. Examples: a football kicked by a player, a ball thrown by a cricketer, a missile fired from a launching pad.
Explanation: the motion is resolved into horizontal and vertical components, which are independent of each other.
A projectile is fired with velocity vi at angle θ with the horizontal; its components are vix = vi cos θ and viy = vi sin θ.
Horizontal motion: neglecting air resistance no horizontal force acts, so ax = 0 and the horizontal velocity stays constant:
vfx = vix = vi cos θ, and horizontal distance x = vix t
Vertical motion: gravity acts downward, so ay = -g (taking upward positive):
vfy = vi sin θ - gt
Velocity at any instant: v = √(vfx² + vfy²), at angle φ with the horizontal, tan φ = vfy/vfx.
A ball thrown horizontally from a height: x = vx t and it falls y = ½gt², like a freely falling body.
The path of a projectile is a parabola. Its height, time of flight and range are
h = vi² sin²θ / 2g, T = 2vi sin θ / g, R = (vi²/g) sin 2θ (maximum at θ = 45°).

blocks.prompt:
2.5 Derive the following expressions for projectile motion:
(i) time of flight
(ii) height attained
(iii) range for projectile.
blocks.explanation:
A projectile is fired with velocity vi at angle θ with the horizontal: vix = vi cos θ, viy = vi sin θ; vertical acceleration = -g, horizontal acceleration = 0.
(i) Time of flight (time to return to the same level): vertical displacement S = 0.
S = viy t - ½gt²
0 = vi sin θ t - ½gt²
t = 2vi sin θ / g
(ii) Height attained: at the highest point vfy = 0. Using 2aS = vf² - vi² with a = -g, S = h:
-2gh = 0 - vi² sin²θ
h = vi² sin²θ / 2g
(iii) Range: horizontal velocity × time of flight
R = vix × t = vi cos θ × 2vi sin θ / g
R = (vi²/g) 2 sin θ cos θ
R = (vi²/g) sin 2θ
R is maximum when sin 2θ = 1, i.e. θ = 45°: Rmax = vi²/g.

blocks.prompt: 2.6 Explain elastic collision in one dimension. Show that relative velocities before and after collision are the same.
blocks.explanation:
Two smooth, non-rotating balls of masses m₁ and m₂ move along the same straight line with velocities v₁ and v₂ (v₁ > v₂). They collide elastically and move along the same line with velocities v₁′ and v₂′. Take the right as positive.
Conservation of momentum:
m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v₁′ + m₂v₂′
m₁(v₁ - v₁′) = m₂(v₂′ - v₂) ...... (1)
Conservation of K.E. (elastic collision):
½m₁v₁² + ½m₂v₂² = ½m₁v₁′² + ½m₂v₂′²
m₁(v₁² - v₁′²) = m₂(v₂′² - v₂²)
m₁(v₁ + v₁′)(v₁ - v₁′) = m₂(v₂′ + v₂)(v₂′ - v₂) ...... (2)
Dividing (2) by (1):
v₁ + v₁′ = v₂′ + v₂
v₁ - v₂ = v₂′ - v₁′ = -(v₁′ - v₂′)
(v₁ - v₂) is the velocity of the first ball relative to the second before the collision and (v₁′ - v₂′) after it. They have the same magnitude but opposite direction: relative velocity of approach = relative velocity of separation.
Solving (1) and (2):
v₁′ = ((m₁ - m₂)/(m₁ + m₂))v₁ + (2m₂/(m₁ + m₂))v₂
v₂′ = (2m₁/(m₁ + m₂))v₁ + ((m₂ - m₁)/(m₁ + m₂))v₂
Special cases: m₁ = m₂: the balls exchange velocities; m₁ = m₂, v₂ = 0: v₁′ = 0, v₂′ = v₁; light ball on a massive ball at rest: v₁′ = -v₁, v₂′ = 0; massive ball on a light ball at rest: v₁′ ≈ v₁, v₂′ ≈ 2v₁.

blocks.prompt: 2.7 Derive the equations for momentum and energy conservation in a two dimensional collision.
blocks.explanation:
Consider an elastic glancing (not head-on) collision. Projectile m₁ moves along the x-axis with velocity v₁i; target m₂ is at rest (v₂i = 0). After the collision m₁ moves with v₁f at angle θ₁ above the x-axis and m₂ with v₂f at angle θ₂ below it.
Resolve the final momenta: m₁v₁f cos θ₁ and m₁v₁f sin θ₁; m₂v₂f cos θ₂ and m₂v₂f sin θ₂.
Conservation of momentum along the x-axis (momentum before = momentum after):
m₁v₁i = m₁v₁f cos θ₁ + m₂v₂f cos θ₂
m₁v₁i - m₁v₁f cos θ₁ = m₂v₂f cos θ₂ ...... (1)
Conservation of momentum along the y-axis (initial y-momentum is zero):
0 = m₁v₁f sin θ₁ - m₂v₂f sin θ₂
m₁v₁f sin θ₁ = m₂v₂f sin θ₂ ...... (2)
Conservation of kinetic energy (elastic collision):
½m₁v₁i² = ½m₁v₁f² + ½m₂v₂f²
m₁v₁i² = m₁v₁f² + m₂v₂f² ...... (3)
There are four unknowns (v₁f, v₂f, θ₁, θ₂); if they are measured, equations (1), (2) and (3) prove the conservation of momentum and energy. (Example: Example 2.9, 1 kg at 5 m s⁻¹ on 1 kg at rest: momentum 5 kg m s⁻¹ and K.E. 12.5 J before and after.)

blocks.prompt: 2.8 Explain an inelastic collision in two dimension.
blocks.explanation:
In a perfectly inelastic collision the colliding bodies stick together; momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not.
Two bodies m₁ and m₂ move in the xy-plane with velocities v₁i (at angle θ₁ with the x-axis) and v₂i (at angle θ₂) and collide at the origin. After the collision they stick together: combined mass M = m₁ + m₂ moving with velocity vf at angle φ with the x-axis.
Momentum in the x-direction:
m₁v₁i cos θ₁ + m₂v₂i cos θ₂ = M vf cos φ ...... (1)
Momentum in the y-direction:
m₁v₁i sin θ₁ + m₂v₂i sin θ₂ = M vf sin φ ...... (2)
Magnitude of the final velocity (squaring and adding (1) and (2)):
vf = √([(m₁v₁i cos θ₁ + m₂v₂i cos θ₂)/M]² + [(m₁v₁i sin θ₁ + m₂v₂i sin θ₂)/M]²)
Direction (dividing (2) by (1)):
φ = tan⁻¹[(m₁v₁i sin θ₁ + m₂v₂i sin θ₂)/(m₁v₁i cos θ₁ + m₂v₂i cos θ₂)]
Kinetic energy (a scalar, so velocities are not resolved):
(K.E)i = ½m₁v₁i² + ½m₂v₂i², (K.E)f = ½M vf²
Loss of K.E. = (K.E)i - (K.E)f; this energy changes into heat, sound and deformation.
Examples: a karate chop breaking bricks, a car crash, a bat hitting a ball.

blocks.prompt: 2.1 The magnitude of cross and scalar products of two vectors are 4√3 and 4, respectively. Find the angle between the vectors. (Ans: 60°)
blocks.explanation:
Given: |A × B| = AB sin θ = 4√3, A.B = AB cos θ = 4
Required: θ
Dividing: AB sin θ / AB cos θ = 4√3 / 4
tan θ = √3
θ = tan⁻¹(√3) = 60°
This agrees with the book's answer.

blocks.prompt: 2.2 A helicopter is ascending vertically at the rate of 19.6 m s⁻¹. When it is at a height of 156.8 m above the ground, a stone is dropped. How long does the stone take to reach the ground? (Ans: 8.0 s)
blocks.explanation:
Given: the stone has the helicopter's velocity when dropped: vi = +19.6 m s⁻¹ (upward positive), a = -g = -9.8 m s⁻², displacement S = -156.8 m (it ends below the starting point)
Required: time t
S = vit + ½at²
-156.8 = 19.6 t - 4.9 t²
4.9 t² - 19.6 t - 156.8 = 0
Dividing by 4.9: t² - 4t - 32 = 0
(t - 8)(t + 4) = 0
t = 8.0 s (t = -4 s has no meaning)
This agrees with the book's answer.

blocks.prompt: 2.3 If |A+B| = |A-B|, then prove that A and B are perpendicular to each other. (Ans: θ = 90°)
blocks.explanation:
Let θ be the angle between A and B.
|A + B|² = (A + B).(A + B) = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ
|A - B|² = (A - B).(A - B) = A² + B² - 2AB cos θ
Given |A + B| = |A - B|, so
A² + B² + 2AB cos θ = A² + B² - 2AB cos θ
4AB cos θ = 0
cos θ = 0 (A and B are not zero)
θ = 90°: A and B are perpendicular.
This agrees with the book's answer.

blocks.prompt: 2.4 A body of mass M at rest explodes into 3 pieces, two of which of mass M/4 each are thrown off in perpendicular directions with velocities of 3 m s⁻¹ and 4 m s⁻¹ respectively. Find the velocity of 3rd piece with which it will be flown away. (Ans: 2.5 m s⁻¹, opposite to resultant velocity vector of two pieces)
blocks.explanation:
Given: initial momentum = 0 (body at rest); m₁ = m₂ = M/4, v₁ = 3 m s⁻¹, v₂ = 4 m s⁻¹ (perpendicular)
Mass of 3rd piece m₃ = M - M/4 - M/4 = M/2
Required: v₃
p₁ = (M/4)(3 m s⁻¹) = 0.75M; p₂ = (M/4)(4 m s⁻¹) = 1.0M (in kg m s⁻¹ when M is in kg)
Resultant momentum of the two pieces = √(p₁² + p₂²) = √(0.75² + 1.0²) M = 1.25M
By conservation of momentum the total momentum stays zero, so the 3rd piece has momentum 1.25M opposite to this resultant:
m₃v₃ = 1.25M
(M/2) v₃ = 1.25M
v₃ = 2.5 m s⁻¹, opposite to the resultant velocity vector of the two pieces
This agrees with the book's answer.

blocks.prompt:
2.6 A cricket ball is hit upward at an angle of 45° with velocity of 20 m s⁻¹. Find its:
(a) time of flight (b) maximum height (c) how far away it hits the ground
(Ans: 2.9 s, 41 m, 10.2 m)
blocks.explanation:
Given: vi = 20 m s⁻¹, θ = 45°, g = 9.8 m s⁻²
(a) Time of flight
t = 2vi sin θ / g = 2 × 20 m s⁻¹ × sin 45° / 9.8 m s⁻² = 28.28 / 9.8 s
t = 2.9 s
(b) Maximum height
h = vi² sin²θ / 2g = (20 m s⁻¹)² × (sin 45°)² / (2 × 9.8 m s⁻²) = 400 × 0.5 / 19.6 m
h = 10.2 m
(c) Range (how far it hits the ground)
R = (vi²/g) sin 2θ = (20 m s⁻¹)² × sin 90° / 9.8 m s⁻² = 400 / 9.8 m
R = 40.8 m ≈ 41 m

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the answers as (2.9 s, 41 m, 10.2 m), in the order (a), (b), (c). The maximum height (b) is 10.2 m and the range (c) is 41 m; the last two answers are printed in each other's place.

blocks.prompt: 2.7 A 20 g ball hits the wall of a squash court with a constant force of 50 N. If the time of impact of force is 0.50 s, find the impulse. (Ans: 25 N s)
blocks.explanation:
Given: F = 50 N, t = 0.50 s (the mass 20 g is not needed)
Required: impulse I
I = F × t
I = 50 N × 0.50 s
I = 25 N s
This agrees with the book's answer.

blocks.prompt:
2.8 A ball is kicked by a footballer. The average force on the ball is 240 N, and the impact lasts for a time interval of 0.25 s. Calculate:
(a) change in momentum
(b) state direction of change in momentum (the direction of change in momentum is the same as the direction of applied force, which is the direction, the footballer kicked the ball) (Ans: 60 N)
blocks.explanation:
Given: F = 240 N, t = 0.25 s
Required: change in momentum Δp and its direction
(a) Δp = mvf - mvi = F × t
Δp = 240 N × 0.25 s
Δp = 60 N s = 60 kg m s⁻¹
(b) Momentum is a vector; the change in momentum is in the direction of the applied force, i.e. in the direction in which the footballer kicked the ball.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the answer as 60 N. Change in momentum = force × time = 240 N × 0.25 s = 60 N s (= 60 kg m s⁻¹); newton is the unit of force, not of momentum.

blocks.prompt: 2.9 An aeroplane moving horizontally at a speed of 200 m s⁻¹ at a height of 8 km to drop a bomb on a target. Find horizontal distance from the target should the bomb be released. (Ans: 8.08 km)
blocks.explanation:
Given: vx = 200 m s⁻¹ (bomb's horizontal velocity = plane's velocity), initial vertical velocity = 0, height y = 8 km = 8000 m, g = 9.8 m s⁻²
Required: horizontal distance x
Vertical motion: y = ½gt²
t = √(2y/g) = √(2 × 8000 m / 9.8 m s⁻²) = √1632.7 s = 40.4 s
Horizontal motion: x = vx × t
x = 200 m s⁻¹ × 40.4 s = 8081 m
x = 8.08 km
This agrees with the book's answer.

blocks.prompt: 2.10 Why does range of a projectile remain the same when angle of projection is changed from θ to θ′ = 90 - θ. Also show that for complementary angles of projection the ratio R/R′ is equal to 1.
blocks.explanation:
Range depends on sin 2θ, and sin 2θ has the same value for θ and 90° - θ, so the range stays the same.
R = (vi²/g) sin 2θ
R′ = (vi²/g) sin 2(90° - θ) = (vi²/g) sin (180° - 2θ) = (vi²/g) sin 2θ (since sin (180° - x) = sin x)
R/R′ = sin 2θ / sin 2θ = 1
Example: 30° and 60° give the same range; the larger angle goes higher and stays longer in the air.
